lessons.title: Determining Harvest Maturity
lessons.body: Soybean harvest maturity is not just about the calendar. You need to check the crop itself. The best time to harvest is when 95% of the pods are brown or tan and the seeds rattle inside. The leaves have mostly dropped, and the stems are dry but not brittle. If you wait too long, pods split open and seeds fall to the ground. If you harvest too early, seeds are green, small, and have poor oil content. In Africa, where many farmers grow soybean in rain-fed conditions, maturity can vary by field and even within a field. Walk your field and sample a few plants from different spots. Squeeze a pod: if the seed is hard and makes a sound, it's ready. A moisture meter is ideal: grain moisture should be between 13% and 15% for harvest. If you don't have a meter, bite a seed: it should crack, not be chewy. In northern Nigeria, harvest often starts in late October to early November; in Zambia, it's May to June. Plan to harvest as soon as the crop is ready, because delays increase losses. If you have a lot of acreage, you may need to harvest in stages. Also, check the weather forecast: if rain is coming, harvest immediately, even if slightly immature, because wet pods lead to mold and poor quality. For smallholders, hand harvesting with sickles is common, but it's slow. If you can, hire a combine harvester or a contractor. The key is to monitor your crop daily once it starts turning brown. Don't rely on neighbours; every field is different. Use a simple moisture tester or the bite test. Harvest when the majority of pods are dry and seeds are firm. This ensures maximum yield and quality.

lessons.title: Combine Settings and Harvest Efficiency
lessons.body: If you use a combine harvester, correct settings are critical to avoid losses. Start with the reel speed: it should be about 10-20% faster than the ground speed. If the reel is too fast, it will beat the pods and cause shattering. For soybean, the cylinder speed should be around 400-600 rpm, and the concave clearance should be wide enough to avoid cracking seeds but narrow enough to thresh all pods. A good starting point is 10-15 mm clearance. The fan speed should be adjusted so that chaff is blown out but seeds are not. Too much air blows seeds out the back; too little leaves chaff in the grain tank. Check the grain tank sample: if you see cracked seeds, reduce cylinder speed or increase clearance. If you see unthreshed pods, tighten clearance or increase speed. Ground speed should be slow enough to allow the header to pick up all pods, but fast enough for efficiency. In Africa, many farmers use small combine harvesters or contractors. Before harvesting, level the field and remove obstacles. Make sure the header is set low to catch low pods, but not so low that it picks up soil. For soybean, the header height should be about 5-10 cm above the ground. If the crop is lodged, you may need to adjust the reel to lift the plants. Always monitor losses behind the combine: place a 1m x 1m sheet on the ground and count seeds. More than 4-5 seeds per square foot means you are losing too much. Adjust settings accordingly. Also, check for header loss: pods left on the stem. If you find many, slow down or adjust the reel. Remember, a well-adjusted combine can reduce losses from 10% to less than 3%. Take time to calibrate. If you are hiring a contractor, insist on a test run and check the grain tank and ground losses. Efficiency saves money and increases your harvest.

lessons.title: Minimizing Harvest Losses
lessons.body: Harvest losses in soybean can be as high as 20% if you are not careful. The main causes are shattering, header loss, and threshing loss. Shattering happens when pods are overly dry and brittle. To reduce it, harvest when moisture is 13-15%, not lower. If you must harvest at lower moisture, do it in the early morning or late evening when humidity is higher, reducing shattering. For hand harvesting, use a sharp sickle and cut close to the ground, then gently place plants on a tarpaulin. Don't throw them. For combine harvesting, adjust the reel speed and height. Also, ensure the header is not too low to avoid picking up stones and soil. Another major loss is from lodging (plants fallen over). If your crop is lodged, you may need to harvest in one direction or use a pickup reel. In Africa, many smallholders harvest by hand and then thresh by beating with sticks. This can cause seed damage and loss. Instead, use a small thresher or a mechanical thresher. If beating, do it on a clean tarpaulin and gently. After threshing, winnow to remove chaff. Losses also occur during transport: use tight bags and don't overload. Store in a dry place. To measure losses, use a 1m x 1m frame. Count seeds on the ground before harvest (pre-harvest loss), during harvest (header loss), and after (threshing loss). Aim for total losses below 5%. For every 1% loss, you lose about 20 kg per hectare if yield is 2 tons. So, 5% loss is 100 kg. That's money lost. Simple steps: harvest at right moisture, adjust combine, use tarpaulins, handle gently. Also, train your workers. In many African communities, sharing a combine or thresher with neighbours can reduce costs and improve efficiency. But ensure the machine is clean to avoid mixing varieties. By minimizing losses, you increase your income and food security.

lessons.title: Drying and Storage of Soybeans
lessons.body: After harvest, soybean moisture is often 15-18%. For safe storage, you need to dry it to 12% or less. If you store at higher moisture, mold grows and seeds rot. In Africa, sun drying is common. Spread beans on a clean tarpaulin or concrete floor in thin layers (5-10 cm) and stir every hour. It takes 2-3 days of good sunshine to reach 12%. If you have a moisture meter, test daily. Without a meter, bite a seed: it should shatter, not be soft. Another method is using a solar dryer or a mechanical dryer. For small quantities, a simple solar dryer with a black plastic sheet can work. Never dry on bare ground; it picks up soil and stones. Also, avoid drying on roads where vehicles may run over. Once dry, clean the beans by winnowing or using a sieve to remove chaff, dirt, and broken seeds. Then store in clean, dry bags. Use new or well-cleaned jute or polypropylene bags. Never use bags that previously held fertilizer or chemicals. Store in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place. Raise bags on pallets or wooden planks to avoid moisture from the floor. Keep away from walls. Stack bags no more than 10 high to avoid crushing. If you have many bags, leave space between stacks for air circulation. For long-term storage, you can use hermetic bags (like PICS bags) or metal silos. These prevent insects and mold. Check stored beans every month for signs of insects or moisture. If you see weevils, you can sun-dry again or use approved storage insecticides like Actellic. But always follow safety instructions. In humid areas, consider using airtight containers. Proper drying and storage can keep soybeans for 6-12 months without quality loss. This allows you to sell when prices are better, not immediately after harvest when prices are low. So invest time in drying and storage.

lessons.title: Grain Quality Standards and Grading
lessons.body: Soybean quality determines its price and use. Buyers look for specific standards: moisture content, foreign matter, broken seeds, and damaged seeds. In most African markets, the standard for Grade 1 soybean is: moisture max 12%, foreign matter max 1%, broken seeds max 2%, and damaged seeds max 3%. Grade 2 allows moisture up to 14%, foreign matter up to 2%, broken up to 5%, damaged up to 5%. Grade 3 is lower. To get a good price, aim for Grade 1. To achieve this, start with a clean harvest. Remove all stones, dirt, and plant parts. Use a sieve or winnowing. Broken seeds come from rough threshing or poor combine settings. Adjust your thresher to minimize breakage. Damaged seeds include those with insect holes, mold, or discoloration. These reduce quality and can cause rejection. After drying, take a sample to a local extension officer or buyer to test. Many cooperatives have moisture meters and grading charts. If you are selling to a processor, they may have specific requirements. For example, some want large seeds for food, others want high oil content for crushing. Know your market. Also, avoid mixing old and new beans; it lowers quality. Store different varieties separately. When bagging, label with date and variety. If you are in a group, consider collective grading and marketing to get better prices. In Nigeria, the Nigerian Agricultural Quarantine Service sets standards; in Kenya, KEBS. But even without formal grading, you can improve by cleaning and drying properly. Remember, a clean, dry product always fetches more. Also, never use chemicals directly on the grain unless approved and correctly applied. Some farmers use storage pesticides, but they must be food-safe. Always read labels. By meeting quality standards, you can access better markets, including export. So, take the extra step to grade your soybean.

lessons.title: Transportation and Marketing Preparation
lessons.body: After harvest, drying, and grading, you need to transport and market your soybean. Proper preparation ensures you get the best price. First, package your beans in clean, strong bags. Use 50 kg or 100 kg bags, depending on the market. For export, 50 kg is common. Make sure bags are sealed and labeled with your name, variety, and weight. If you are selling to a cooperative or processor, they may provide bags. Otherwise, buy new polypropylene bags. Avoid overfilling; leave a small space for tying. Before transport, arrange for a vehicle. For small quantities, use a pickup or a lorry. For larger, hire a truck. Ensure the vehicle is clean and dry. Cover with a tarpaulin to protect from rain and dust. If traveling long distances, avoid delays because heat and humidity can affect quality. In Africa, poor roads can cause bruising and breakage. So, pack bags tightly to reduce movement. Also, consider the timing: market prices are usually lowest at harvest and rise later. If you can store safely, sell 3-6 months later when prices are higher. But you need to monitor market trends. Join a farmer group or cooperative to access market information and better prices. Many cooperatives aggregate and negotiate with buyers. Also, get a moisture meter or have your beans tested before sale. Buyers will test and may reject if moisture is above 12%. For marketing, know your buyer: local traders, processors, or export companies. Each has different requirements. For export, you may need certification (e.g., phytosanitary certificate) and meet aflatoxin standards. Aflatoxin is a poison from mold; proper drying and storage prevent it. If you suspect mold, don't sell for food. Also, keep records of your production and sales for future planning. Finally, consider value addition: cleaning, grading, or even processing into oil or feed can increase income. But start with proper transportation and marketing preparation. With good planning, you can turn your soybean into a profitable venture.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Harvesting & Post-Harvest Handling of Soybean in Africa

Soybean is one of Africa's fastest-growing cash and food crops, driven by demand from poultry feed millers, edible oil processors, and smallholder nutrition programmes. Yet the gap between potential yield and marketable grain often comes down to what happens in the two weeks around harvest. Poor timing, wrong combine settings, inadequate drying, or bad storage can cut saleable value by 20â40% and destroy the premium that processors pay for quality grain. This Practical Reference gives you the operating numbers, thresholds, and checklists you need to protect margin from field to buyer.

1. Determining Harvest Maturity

Harvest too early and you get green, shrivelled seed with low oil content and poor germination. Harvest too late and pods shatter, seed splits, and you lose 5â15% before the combine reaches the field. The commercial trigger is simple: 95% of pods are brown or tan, and seed moisture has dropped to 13â15%. At this point, seed in the pod rattles when shaken. In most African growing zones â from Nigeria's Benue State to Zambia's Eastern Province â this window is 7â10 days wide. After that, shatter loss accelerates sharply, especially in indeterminate varieties.

Walk the field diagonally and sample 10 plants from 5 points. If more than 5% of pods are still green, wait 2â3 days. If leaves have dropped and stems are dry but pods are still green, you may be looking at a variety with delayed maturity â check with your seed supplier. For seed production, harvest at 12â13% moisture to protect germination above 85%.

2. Combine Settings and Harvest Efficiency

Most smallholder and medium-scale African soybean is still harvested by hand or with tractor-mounted reapers, but combine use is rising in Zambia, South Africa, and Nigeria's commercial belt. The table below gives starting settings for a conventional combine; adjust by 10â15% based on variety, moisture, and field conditions.

Table 1: Starting combine settings for soybean (conventional cylinder combine)
Parameter Setting Notes
Cylinder speed400â600 rpmLower for dry crop, higher for tough or green stems
Concave clearance6â10 mm front, 4â8 mm rearToo tight = cracked seed; too wide = unthreshed pods
Fan speed650â850 rpmIncrease in light crop, decrease in heavy or damp crop
Ground speed4â6 km/hSlow enough to keep header full but not overloaded
Reel speed1.1â1.3Ã ground speedFaster reel causes shatter; slower causes feeding issues
Header height5â10 cm above groundCut low enough to catch lowest pods
Loss target<3% totalCheck behind combine with a 1 mÂ² frame

Source: adapted from FAO (2017), Save and Grow: A policymaker's guide to sustainable intensification of smallholder crop production; and Iowa State University Extension (2020), Soybean Harvest Tips.

3. Minimizing Harvest Losses

Losses in African soybean harvest typically run 8â20% combined. The biggest culprits are shatter at the header, unthreshed pods, and cracked seed from over-threshing. To cut losses:

  • Harvest at the right moisture. 13â15% is the sweet spot. Below 12% shatter risk rises; above 16% you get clogging and mould.
  • Harvest early morning or late afternoon. Dew reduces shatter. Avoid the hottest part of the day.
  • Slow down. A 20% reduction in ground speed can cut header loss by half.
  • Check behind the combine every 2 hours. Use a 1 mÂ² frame and count seeds on the ground. More than 4 seeds/mÂ² means adjust settings.
  • Use a stripper header or air reel where available â these reduce shatter significantly in dry conditions.
  • Train operators. A well-trained combine operator can save 3â5% of the crop, which on a 5-tonne crop is 150â250 kg â real money.

4. Drying and Storage of Soybeans

After harvest, soybean must be dried to 12â13% moisture for safe storage of up to 6 months, and to 11â12% for longer storage or seed. In humid African zones â the Guinea Savannah, the Congo Basin, coastal West Africa â natural sun drying on tarpaulins can take 3â5 days. In drier zones like the Sudan Savannah or Zambia's plateau, 2â3 days is often enough.

Key rules:

  • Never dry on bare ground â soil, stones, and animal droppings contaminate the grain and downgrade it at the buying centre.
  • Spread to 5 cm depth and turn every 2 hours for even drying.
  • Use a moisture meter. Cheap handheld meters cost $30â80 and pay for themselves in one season.
  • Cool grain before storage. Hot grain in bags causes condensation and mould.
  • Use hermetic storage (PICS bags, GrainPro, or metal silos) to control insects without chemicals. This is now the gold standard across Africa.
  • Stack bags on pallets, 10 cm off the floor and 20 cm from walls. Never stack against a damp wall.

5. Grain Quality Standards and Grading

Processors and feed millers in Africa increasingly grade soybean, and price differentials between Grade 1 and Grade 3 can be 15â30%. The table below summarises the key parameters used by most national bureaus of standards and regional processors.

Table 2: Typical soybean grading parameters in African markets (Grade 1 vs Grade 3)
Parameter Grade 1 Grade 2 Grade 3
Moisture contentâ¤12%â¤13%â¤14%
Foreign matterâ¤1%â¤2%â¤3%
Broken/split seedsâ¤2%â¤4%â¤6%
Discoloured/damagedâ¤2%â¤4%â¤6%
Live insectsNilNilNil
Oil content (as received)â¥18%â¥17%â¥16%
Protein contentâ¥36%â¥34%â¥32%

Source: adapted from East African Community (EAC) EAS 758:2019 â Soybean grains specification; and Nigerian Stored Products Research Institute (NSPRI) post-harvest quality guidelines.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Grain dust and fumigation hazards

Soybean dust is highly combustible and can cause severe respiratory irritation. Always wear a dust mask and eye protection when handling, cleaning, or bagging grain. Never smoke or use open flames near grain dust. If you use phosphine fumigation tablets for storage insect control, they are highly toxic â only trained and licensed operators should apply them, and the store must be sealed, signed, and kept locked for the full fumigation period (typically 5â7 days). Never enter a fumigated store without a gas monitor and self-contained breathing apparatus. In many African countries, phosphine use is restricted to licensed pest control operators. For smallholder storage, hermetic bags (PICS/GrainPro) are the safer alternative and are approved across the continent.

6. Transportation and Marketing Preparation

Your grain's value is set at the point of sale, and buyers discount heavily for poor presentation. Before you load:

  • Clean the grain. Remove stones, chaff, and broken seed. A simple winnowing or a small cleaner can move you from Grade 3 to Grade 1.
  • Use clean, dry bags. Never use bags that previously held fertiliser or chemicals. Use new or properly washed polypropylene bags of 50 kg or 100 kg.
  • Label each bag with your name, farm, date, variety, and moisture content. This builds trust with processors and can earn a premium.
  • Transport in covered vehicles. Rain or damp tarpaulins can add 2â3% moisture in transit and cause mould within days.
  • Deliver at the right moisture. Buyers test on arrival. If your grain is above 13%, you may be rejected or heavily discounted.
  • Aggregate with neighbours to meet minimum volumes (often 5â20 tonnes) required by processors and to negotiate better prices.
  • Know your market. Feed millers want high protein; oil processors want high oil. Test your grain and target the buyer who values your specific quality.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Harvest when 95% of pods are brown and seed moisture is 13â15%.
  2. Set combine cylinder at 400â600 rpm and check loss behind the machine every 2 hours.
  3. Harvest early morning or late afternoon to reduce shatter.
  4. Dry on tarpaulins to 12â13% moisture; never on bare ground.
  5. Use a moisture meter before storage and before sale.
  6. Store in hermetic bags or silos, off the floor and away from walls.
  7. Clean and grade grain before bagging to reach Grade 1 or 2.
  8. Label bags and transport in covered vehicles to protect quality.

Further Reading

  • FAO â The State of Food and Agriculture 2019: Moving forward on food loss and waste reduction (free PDF)
  • IITA â Soybean Production and Processing in Africa (free PDF)
  • East African Community â EAS 758:2019 Soybean grains specification (free standard summary)
  • Nigerian Stored Products Research Institute (NSPRI) â Post-harvest guidelines (free resources)
  • Iowa State University Extension â Soybean Harvest Tips (free technical articles)

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for soybean harvest?
quiz.explanation: Harvesting at 13-15% moisture reduces shattering and seed damage.

quiz.q: Which test can a farmer use to check if soybean is ready for harvest without a moisture meter?
options: B) Bite a seed; it should crack
quiz.explanation: A hard seed that cracks when bitten indicates maturity.

quiz.q: What is the recommended cylinder speed for a combine harvesting soybean?
quiz.explanation: 400-600 rpm threshes pods without cracking too many seeds.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a combine is losing too many seeds out the back?
options: B) More than 4-5 seeds per square foot behind the combine
quiz.explanation: Counting seeds on the ground helps measure and adjust losses.

quiz.q: Which practice helps reduce shattering during hand harvesting?
options: B) Harvest when pods are very dry
C) Harvest in early morning or late evening
D) Throw plants onto a pile
quiz.explanation: Higher humidity in early morning or evening makes pods less brittle.

quiz.q: What is the maximum acceptable total harvest loss for good management?
quiz.explanation: Aim for less than 5% total loss to maximize yield.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid drying soybeans on bare ground?
options: B) It picks up soil and stones
quiz.explanation: Bare ground contaminates beans with dirt and stones, lowering quality.

quiz.q: What is the safe moisture content for storing soybeans?
quiz.explanation: At 12% or less, mold and insect growth are minimized.

quiz.q: Which type of bag is best for long-term storage to prevent insects?
quiz.explanation: Hermetic bags create an airtight environment that kills insects.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored soybeans?
quiz.explanation: Monthly checks help detect moisture or insect problems early.

quiz.q: What is the maximum foreign matter allowed for Grade 1 soybean?
quiz.explanation: Grade 1 standards typically allow only 1% foreign matter.

quiz.q: Which factor is NOT part of soybean grading standards?
quiz.explanation: Color is not usually a grading factor; moisture, foreign matter, and damage are.

quiz.q: What causes aflatoxin in soybeans?
options: B) Mold growth due to high moisture
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is produced by molds when moisture is high during storage.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing old and new soybean?
quiz.explanation: Old beans may have lower quality, reducing the grade of the whole lot.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bag size for soybean export?
quiz.explanation: 50 kg bags are standard for many export markets.

quiz.q: How can you protect soybean bags during transport?
quiz.explanation: A tarpaulin protects from rain and dust, maintaining quality.

quiz.q: When are soybean prices usually lowest?
quiz.explanation: Supply is high at harvest, so prices are typically low.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a cooperative for marketing?
options: A) Better prices through collective bargaining
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives can negotiate better prices and access larger markets.

quiz.q: What should you do before selling soybean to a buyer?
options: A) Add water to increase weight
quiz.explanation: Buyers test moisture; knowing your moisture helps avoid rejection.

quiz.q: Which of these is a value addition activity for soybean?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and grading increase market value.

quiz.q: What is the first sign that soybean is ready to harvest?
options: B) 95% of pods are brown or tan
quiz.explanation: Brown pods and rattling seeds indicate maturity.

quiz.q: What should you do if rain is forecast before harvest?
options: A) Wait for rain to pass
quiz.explanation: Rain can cause mold and shattering, so harvest early if possible.

quiz.q: What is the recommended header height for combine harvesting soybean?
quiz.explanation: Low header catches low pods but avoids soil.

quiz.q: What causes broken seeds during threshing?
quiz.explanation: High cylinder speed cracks or breaks seeds.

quiz.q: How can you reduce harvest loss from lodging?
quiz.explanation: Harvesting in one direction helps pick up lodged plants.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of winnowing after threshing?
options: A) To remove chaff and dirt
quiz.explanation: Winnowing separates lighter chaff from heavier seeds.

quiz.q: Which storage practice helps prevent moisture from the floor?
options: B) Place bags directly on floor
quiz.explanation: Pallets raise bags, avoiding moisture absorption from the floor.

quiz.q: What is the maximum moisture content for Grade 2 soybean?
quiz.explanation: Grade 2 allows up to 14% moisture.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label bags with date and variety?
options: A) For traceability and quality control
quiz.explanation: Labels help track storage time and maintain identity.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect aflatoxin in your soybean?
options: B) Do not sell for food; seek advice
D) Use as animal feed without testing
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is dangerous; do not sell contaminated beans for human consumption.
